newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba moves against illegal renting, tax evasion.
newsitem.headline: Cuba moves against illegal renting, tax evasion.

text.p: A public call by President Fidel Castro has moved Cuban officials to begin cracking down on illegal house rentals, tax evasion and other examples of "social indiscipline," state media reported on Friday.

Cuban radio and newspapers cited a recent meeting involving senior government figures who discussed new laws that would regulate the renting of private houses and control the migration of citizens from rural areas to the capital.

The laws, which would be put into effect shortly, followed a tough speech by Castro this month in which he called for a nationwide crackdown of growing illegal economic activity and "social indiscipline."

"We need laws, rules and inspectors," Cuban Vice President Carlos Lage said at the meeting attended by members of Cuba's Committees for the Defence of the Revolution (CDR), the neighbourhood block committees responsible for implementing official policies at the local level.

The Decree Law to regulate the widespread practice of renting private accommodations would require landlords to pay taxes on their rental earnings and officially register themselves and their tenants. Only homeowners would be allowed to rent out accommodations.

Another law, already approved by the government but still awaiting publication, would seek to control the flow of migration from the interior of the communist-ruled island to the capital. It would only apply to Havana but could be extended to other provincial capitals in the future.
The CRD block committees were asked to participate in detecting and eradicating illegal activities, such as tax evaders or private self-employed workers who broke the law.

In an April 4 speech Castro had warned that uncontrolled migration to Havana and a lack of control over housing and self-employment had created growing crime and overcrowding, especially in the capital where more than two million of Cuba's 11 million people live.
